newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesia Balongan refinery problem plagued.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia Balongan refinery problem plagued.

text.p: A shutdown at Indonesia's Balongan oil refinery is the latest in a string of problems that has plagued the $2.0 billion facility since it began production in September 1994, industry sources said on Wednesday.

The latest problem affecting its long residue catalytic cracker (LRCC) was detected after the refinery's first scheduled maintenance shutdown between October 1 and December 2, 1996, said a source with state oil firm Pertamina.
The LRCC was shut down from February 6 as one of the refinery's four functioning boilers failed to reach the required temperature, triggering a leak in one of the pumps.

This paralysed the unit's ability to refine residues into lighter products such as gasoline, diesel and jet-kerosene fuel, forcing Pertamina to keep its crude distillation unit (CDU) shut because its residues tanks are full.

Several attempts to restart the LRCC unit have so far failed. Pertamina now hoped it could be restarted by March 17 at the earliest, while the 125,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) crude unit was set to resume operations two days earlier, the source said.
The source said about 1,500 Pertamina maintenance workers and 60 technical experts from U.S. firm Universal Oil Products, the LRCC licensee processor, were involved in the repair project.
Problems for the West Java refinery began not long after production began in September 1994.
Barely three months after full operations began, the 83,000-bpd LRCC, touted as one of the world's biggest, was crippled by serious technical difficulties that lasted more than four months.
That shutdown was triggered by a block in one of the boiler pumps, the source said.
The problem prompted Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana to issue an ultimatum to the refinery contractors to complete the repairs in six weeks starting from end January 1995.
The unit only resumed normal production in early April 1995, and it was officially opened by President Suharto in May that year.
A series of hiccups involving its boiler followed, the worst of which was an explosion in April last year that shut down one of its five boilers, killed two and injured several workers.
The explosion occurred when the refinery workers were trying to start the boiler when traces of gas were still present and triggered a flare.

The refinery was initiated as Indonesia's first Export-Oriented Refinery (EXOR-1) but the name was dropped in favour of Balongan as domestic demand far exceeded production, making it difficult for the country to export.
The refinery was built by a consortium comprising Japan's JGC, Mitsui & Co, Far East Oil Trading, and Foster Wheeler of the United States.
The construction was funded by Java Petroleum Investment Co Ltd, a consortium consisting of Mitsui, Marubeni Corp, Sumitomo, Itochu Corp and 20 Japanese bankers.

Industry sources said the actual costs resulting from the technical problems were difficult to estimate. But it affected Pertamina's ability to furnish its loan repayment in oil products under a deal with British Petroleum, Itochu and Mitsui.
The current shutdown has also totally stopped Balongan's liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) output, prompting concerns that if it persisted, LPG supplies to Jakarta would be affected.
